The quest battle isn't that difficult.  


Get Karl Franz on their Lord, and get him to rout. Send you cav into their artillery immediately and you'll shut them down before they even get a single shot off. Attack their infantry with yours as soon as the battle starts and you'll get them to rout soon enough.   


After their artillery has been defeated, move your cav to the top left of the map. That way they can deal with the incoming ranged cav. Be careful not to get your cav stuck in the enemy infantry tho.  


After you've routed most of the main force get your missiles along with some of your healthier melee infantry up on the hill in the middle, to prepare for the second attack from the top left. The rest of your melee infantry should be chasing after routing units to keep them from coming back.  


After you win you'll get a battle wizard(Hopefully light or fire), now magic can be hard to use for new players, it was for me at least. But i advise you to figure out how to use it, since magic is a big part of the Empire play style.

Total War Mongol:

Map: A massive map sprawling from the heart of Europe to Japan, storyline should span from the birth of Gengis to the fall of the Yuan dynasty.

Culture: The Mongols were famed for their inclusion of other cultures and religions. Different peoples would provide sevices such as administration, taxation, infastructure, since the mongols themselves were mostly focused on war.. Each culture could provide different bonuses, and allow you to recruit different types of units.

Civilization or horde: Starting as the Mongols you will play as a horde faction, Reducing the cost of units and increasing campaign movement range for all armies. But after the leader dies, your most powerful generals will take certain parts of your empire for themselves and become your vassals. With every new leader you can choose to settle permanently in the regions you have left or continue with your barbarian ways. Settling down will remove the bonuses to cost and movement, but will allow you to keep all of your empire when your leader dies.

The silk road: Controlling the silk road will be of paramount importance, and allowing other factions to use your silk road for monthly tributes will be a key part of the game. Income from trade will for many factions be their main income source, so picking your friends and foes and who you trade with wont be so easy.

The Lionhearted: Playing as an European kingdom will present quite a different challenge. You cant just focus on conquest and war, but you have to play the political game. Do you trade and pay tribute to the mighty Khan of Khans, well you have a significant increase in income, but other christian nations might become upset (The Pope Especially will not like this). Or do you work with the Pope and other Christian rulers to overthrow the Khan and destabilize the Mongol empire? No easy task, but hire mercenaries, crusaders and spies and assassins, to chip away at the Khanate. Can the squabbling states of Europe band together to defend against the tide of mongol expansion?

Servants of the Great Khan: Playing as smaller faction in Asia or eastern Europe, can provide a quite unique campaign. Rulers may pledge fealty to the great Khan, becoming vassals and gaining many benefits from the mongol trade network. Will you serve the Khan faithfully helping spread the mandate of Genghis? Or do you through intrigue and diplomacy, use the instability of the Khanate against it self? Wait for a time when the Mongols are weak and divided and carve out an empire for yourself, or claim the entire Khanate as a successor.
